info.bio: David Byrne nació el 14 de mayo de 1952 en Dumbarton, Escocia. Músico notable, es miembro fundador y compositor de la banda New Wave Talking Heads. Sus padres se mudaron a Canadá cuando David Byrne apenas contaba dos años; posteriormente, con ocho, vivió una nueva mudanza junto a su familia, que decidió establecerse en los suburbios de Baltimore, Maryland (Estados Unidos). En su adolescencia tocó la guitarra en diferentes grupos, pero tan sólo como un pasatiempo.

scenes.name: Funk industrial
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras la caída de P-Funk, muchos ritmos nuevos vinieron de fuera: Kraftwerk, Art of Noise («Beat Box», «Close (to the Edit)»), Talking Heads (Stop Making Sense, con Bernie Worrell) y el «Genius of Love» de Tom Tom Club. Herbie Hancock pidió a su mánager Tony Meilandt unos temas de hip hop y con Bill Laswell y Grandmixer D.S.T. hizo «Rockit» (Future Shock, 1983): la cima del funk industrial nada más empezar. Laswell (Material, Time Zone con John Lydon, Manu Dibango, los Last Poets) dejó su sello de bajo grueso; sellos como Celluloid, On-U Sound, Tommy Boy o Def Jam sacaban ritmos ásperos de raspados metálicos y tensión de Guerra Fría. On-U Sound de Adrian Sherwood fichó a la sección rítmica de Sugarhill (Doug Wimbish, Skip McDonald, Keith LeBlanc): Tackhead, el «No Sell Out» con la voz de Malcolm X, «el P-Funk de los ochenta» según Pedro Bell.

scenes.name: Talking Heads
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Estudiantes de la Escuela de Diseño de Rhode Island que no querían ser llamados art rock: imagen «normal» y pulcra frente al cuero del CBGB, guitarra «finita, limpia y metálica» de David Byrne, el bajo melódico de Tina Weymouth con slap a lo Larry Graham y Jerry Harrison (ex Modern Lovers) a los teclados. Con «Psycho Killer» fundan los nervios de la new wave, pero siempre con funk, tocado como blancos de clase media. Brian Eno, casi un quinto miembro y su George Martin, produce una trilogía de «funk psicodélico» inspirada en Parliament-Funkadelic: More Songs About Buildings and Food («Take Me to the River»), Fear of Music (la desorientación de 1979, «Life During Wartime», «I Zimbra» con un poema de Hugo Ball) y Remain in Light (1980), afrofunk construido con improvisaciones recortadas en el estudio, polirritmo y predicadores radiofónicos: «una obra maestra». Las tensiones por la autoría con Eno llevan a un regreso al pop; Weymouth y Frantz triunfan con Tom Tom Club.
scenes.family: Art punk y new wave americana

scenes.name: Eno, Byrne y el Cuarto Mundo
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Eno, «texturólogo» de las escuelas de arte inglesas (las Oblique Strategies con Peter Schmidt: «Honra tus errores como si ocultaran intenciones secretas»), compone letras como imágenes y concibe el arte como entrenamiento para la incertidumbre. Con David Byrne y la idea del «Cuarto Mundo» de Jon Hassell (tecnología occidental más música étnica) graban My Life in the Bush of Ghosts (1981): funk, música árabe, polirritmos del oeste africano y voces encontradas de predicadores radiofónicos. Acusado de frío y neocolonial, anticipa el sampleo del hip hop, el house y el jungle (Public Enemy, DJ Shadow, Moby).

podcast.title: Early Users of Fairlight CMI (1979 onwards)
podcast.body: David Byrne was among the artists who recognized the innovative potential of the Fairlight CMI digital sampler, introduced in 1979. This technology opened "new possibilities" for him in terms of audio manipulation and creative composition. "Peter Gabriel, Kate Bush, Brian Eno, David Byrne, New Order, and Thomas Dolby all saw new possibilities in the technology."

podcast.title: Admiration for Arcade Fire's Songcraft
podcast.body: David Byrne of The Talking Heads expressed extensive admiration for Arcade Fire's songcraft. He noted that he observed elements of his former band's artsy, semi-world music style from their earlier days reflected in Arcade Fire's work. "David Byrne of The Talking Hints wrote at length about how he admired their song craft and how he heard and saw bits of what his old band used to do in their artsy semi-world music sort of way back in the day."

podcast.title: Asperger's Syndrome Diagnosis
podcast.body: David Byrne has been diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome, a condition on the mild end of the autism spectrum. While two other members of Talking Heads reportedly attributed the band's breakup to Byrne's autism, Byrne acknowledges his diagnosis, stating he has learned to manage it through music, treating it more as a personality trait than a disorder. "Burn has been diagnosed as having Asperger's syndrome, which is on the autism spectrum, mild end, but still."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Distinctive Vocal and Stage Style
podcast.body: Film critic Pauline Kael described Byrne's voice as "not a singer's voice," but rather a shouter's or chanter's, with an emotional, faintly metallic wail that paradoxically never seemed to crack or weaken. His stage presence was marked by constant motion—jiggling, aerobic walking, jumping, and dancing—and a withdrawn, disembodied, sci-fi quality. "Byrne himself is the parodist, and he commands the stage by his hollow wide, frosty verb. Byrne's voice isn't a singer's voice."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Etch-A-Sketch Talent
podcast.body: During breaks between sets at early Talking Heads gigs in New York, David Byrne would entertain patrons at the bar by demonstrating his unique ability to draw a highly detailed map of the United States using an Etch-A-Sketch. "Between sets, David would sit at the bar and show everyone how he could draw a detailed map of the United States with his etch-a-sketch."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Yelping Vocal Style
podcast.body: David Byrne was highly influential in popularizing a distinct "yelping" vocal style that became prominent among some New Wave artists in the early 1980s. This style was also adopted by bands such as Devo and Oingo Boingo, solidifying Byrne's impact on the vocal trends of the era. "Burn was very influential in introducing that yelping sort of singing voice that became very popular with some new waivers in the early 80s."

podcast.title: Pauline Kael's Description
podcast.body: Legendary film critic Pauline Kael of The New York Times described David Byrne as a "parodist" who commanded the stage with a "hollow wide, frosty verb." Kael noted that Byrne's voice, lacking resonance, was more akin to a shouter or chanter, with a "faintly metallic whale," yet it never cracked or weakened despite his constant jiggling, aerobic walking, jumping, and dancing on stage. "Burn himself is the parodist, and he commands the stage by his hollow wide, frosty verb."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Role in Talking Heads Breakup
podcast.body: The dissolution of Talking Heads was, in part, blamed by two other band members on Byrne's autism, indicating its impact on group dynamics. "Two of the other members blamed the death of the group on Byrne's autism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Self-Characterized Asperger Syndrome
podcast.body: David Byrne of the Talking Heads characterizes himself as extremely self-conscious, expressing discomfort with shaking hands and feeling socially awkward. He believes he has borderline Asperger Syndrome, a form of high-functioning autism often linked to above-average intelligence and significant creativity. "He believes he has borderline asperger syndrome, a type of high functioning autism that can lead to above average intelligence mixed with great creativity."

xref.body: Frontman David Byrne was known for being socially awkward in person, later speculating that he might be on the Asperger spectrum. This awkwardness often translated into his stage presence, making him appear quirky, experimental, and occasionally paranoid, yet he was celebrated in the punk era for his authenticity. "In person, he was socially awkward. He later speculated that he's somewhere on the Asperger spectrum and was almost as awkward on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Early Days
xref.body: David Byrne, Chris, and Martino lived together in Rhode Island while attending art school. They eventually formed a group and relocated to New York City, where they spent considerable time performing gigs at a specific "scusy little club" frequented by "cool people." "Eventually, they formed a group and they moved to New York where they spent a lot of time playing gigs at a scusy little club where all the cool people hung out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Very First Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Founding Members' Background
xref.body: Drummer Chris Frantz and bassist Tina Weymouth, a husband-and-wife team, met while attending art school in Rhode Island. They later moved to New York with singer David Byrne in the mid-1970s to form the band. "They met while attending art school in Rhode Island and decided to move to New York with singer David Byrne in the middle 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Arcade Fire's Artistry
xref.body: David Byrne, the frontman of Talking Heads, identified similarities between his band's former artsy, semi-world music approach and Arcade Fire's songcraft, indicating a potential stylistic resonance or influence. "David Byrne of The Talking Hints wrote at length about how he admired their song craft and how he heard and saw bits of what his old band used to do in their artsy semi-world music sort of way back in the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Breakup Projects
xref.body: Following their time with Talking Heads, the members pursued various projects: David Byrne embarked on a solo career, Jerry Harrison also engaged in solo work, and Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth formed the group Tom Tom Club. "David Byrne has a solo career, Jerry Harrison does stuff on his own and Chris and Tina are the Tom Tom Fub."
